free_tier.stated: Free and registration-free: the front page offers Download HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS4, and SOCKS5 proxies without limitations, and the SOCKS5 file held 8,046 lines when harvested on 2026-10-24.
free_tier.notes: Nothing is counted, sold or metered, so the unit is none: the product is a text file of third-party addresses. A second fetch of socks5.txt on the same day returned 7,877 lines against the 8,047 harvested, so the line count moves between fetches.

per_object_cap.stated: not applicable: an address, not an object

retention.stated: not applicable: a list of live addresses, not stored bytes. The vendor states the list is rebuilt every 10 minutes.
retention.notes: The decay that matters is line lifetime, not byte retention: of 60 lines sampled from a same-day snapshot, 12 carried a payload and 46 failed at the handshake.

egress.terms: The vendor publishes no traffic terms because it carries no traffic: each line is a third-party SOCKS5 endpoint and the bytes cross that endpoint's operator, not a vendor network. What the vendor does state, about requests to the list itself, is: No, you can send as many requests as you want. As long as you don't harm our webserver, we don't care.

interface_detail: A plain-text file at /socks5.txt, one host:port per line, served as text/plain with no header row and no field beyond host and port. The front page links four such files (http.txt, https.txt, socks4.txt, socks5.txt) and no API.
tooling: Any HTTP client can download /socks5.txt, followed by SOCKS5 connections via curl using SOCKS5 hostname resolution or custom socket clients. The list is formatted as plaintext host and port entries without proprietary wrappers.
chaining: A disposable exit pool behind a crawler or the AI gateway: draw a line, retry across lines on failure, keep no state. It chains with nothing else because no line carries a country, an ASN, a protocol or an uptime to select on, so the only selection signal a caller has is a failed request.

limits.value: none stated by the vendor: No, you can send as many requests as you want. As long as you don't harm our webserver, we don't care.
none: free, unpriced and unmetered; no byte quota exists because the bytes do not cross a vendor network
unstated and unknowable before use: no line carries a rate, a country, an ASN or an uptime, so the throttling done by the operator behind each address is discovered only by hitting it

limits_note: The constraint that decides this record names no vocabulary kind: yield. Twelve of 60 sampled lines carried a payload (20.0%), and a same-fraction extrapolation over 8,047 lines is about 1,600 addresses, labelled an extrapolation from 60 lines rather than a measurement. The measured pool is smaller again, because the 12 successes sat on 7 distinct addresses.
binding_note: Nothing in the vocabulary fails first at 45 GB a month across 599,000 requests: the list is free, unpriced and states no request limit, so there is no quota or rate to reach. What fails first is yield and address diversity, which the vocabulary has no kind for: 12 of 60 sampled lines carried a payload and those 12 sat on 7 distinct hosts, 6 of them ports on one address.

identity_cost.detail: No registration, no email, no card: the list is fetched directly, and the site's own description states No signup required.

reliability_note: Failures are silent and mostly by timeout: of 60 sampled lines, 35 timed out, 4 answered the SOCKS5 greeting with no acceptable method (authentication demanded), and 1 handshook then returned a Synology DiskStation login page in place of the target body.
confidence_note: Measured: 60 lines were driven through a SOCKS5 handshake and a payload fetch on 2026-10-24, with one row per line in sources/p/bd/bd85efdb7e78591ca3a4078c123a8c90eeb0356d7264bef5482f0823d84e2aa3.json.gz, and the rows were re-counted here (60 rows, 14 handshake, 12 payload) rather than taken from a summary. The rung does not rise with a larger sample: the pool is rebuilt every 10 minutes, so any count is one day's snapshot.

evidence.proved: The site answered 200 with 7,799 bytes and offers four plain-text downloads with no signup; its FAQ states Updated every 10 minutes, All proxies are tested before being listed, and No, you can send as many requests as you want.

Served text/plain at 141,636 bytes, 7,877 lines, each a bare host:port with no protocol, country, ASN, uptime or authentication field; the first three lines match the harvested snapshot, so the harvested file is this list at an earlier moment.

60 lines sampled from the openproxylist/socks5 list: 14 completed a SOCKS5 handshake, 12 carried a payload to an exit IP (20.0%), 35 timed out, 4 returned no acceptable method, 3 EOF, 3 connection refused, 1 reset, 1 an HTML body in place of the target.

The harvested list is 8,046 lines by wc -l and 8,047 host:port entries, because the last line has no trailing newline; all 8,047 are unique and they cover 2,107 distinct addresses, with no metadata on any line.

notes:
Operational characteristics and yield measurements for openproxylist.xyz. The site publishes /socks5.txt containing 8,047 unique host and port entries (measured on 2026-10-24 at 141,636 bytes).

Yield measurements on 2026-10-24: across a 60-line test sample, 12 connections (20.0 percent) successfully delivered HTTP payloads. These 12 successes routed across only 7 distinct IP addresses, with 6 ports terminating on 45.74.31.42. Furthermore, 9 of the 12 working connections exited through upstream IP addresses differing from the listed entry address (exiting via GoDaddy, Contabo, and Google datacenter ranges). Non-working connections failed with 35 timeouts, 3 connection refusals, 3 EOFs, 1 reset, and 4 SOCKS5 authentication rejections.

List composition and duplication: 5,087 of the 8,047 entries (63.2 percent) represent byte-identical host and port pairs shared with the TheSpeedX socks5 repository, indicating aggregated scraping across public proxy lists rather than independent capacity. File entry counts fluctuate with automated 10-minute rebuild cycles.
